title: Off-duty Toronto cop who tackled Brampton student who later died in Kijiji deal gone bad found guilty of assault
subtitle: In her ruling, the judge said she did not believe much of off-duty Toronto Const. Calvin Au's "unreliable" evidence.
article: A Toronto cop was found guilty of assault in a 2021 clash that began with a Kijiji deal gone bad and ended, hours later, in the death of a young Brampton man - an outcome the victim's family said shows off-duty police officers "cannot abuse their power."

In a decision that heaped criticism on the two Toronto cops central to the case, Superior Court Justice Jennifer Woollcombe said she did not believe much of accused Const. Calvin Au's "unreliable" and "bizarre" evidence about why and how he tackled 19-year-old Chadd Facey to the ground in a suburban Brampton park after he sold him a counterfeit Apple watch.

Not only was the force he used unreasonable - both for the petty crime circumstances, and considering the scrawny teen posed no threat and was carrying no weapons - but the judge rejected Au's claim that he'd been making an arrest and would therefore be justified to use necessary force.

But despite her forceful condemnation of Au, Woollcombe said she could not make a definitive finding on the central issue at the trial for assault causing bodily harm: whether Au's takedown of Facey had caused a hematoma, or bruise, on Facey's forehead, as prosecutors alleged.
Though she said the injury was "likely" sustained then, Woollcombe could not rule out that it may have been sustained earlier in the day or after the violent clash.

"I cannot be satisfied, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Au's assault caused the bruise," Woollcombe said, finding Au not guilty of assault causing bodily harm but guilty of the lesser count of assault.

Facey's family, including his mother and sister, had packed into a Brampton court Wednesday to listen to the ruling. A man at one point began to sob quietly, while others appeared stunned following the decision.
Asha James, the lawyer representing the family, said Facey's loved ones respect the decision of the court "but of course they were hoping for more."

"However, for the court to recognize that the actions of Const. Au were not only wrong, but criminal, demonstrates that even off-duty police officers cannot abuse their power and authority," James said.

Au, who had pleaded not guilty, showed no emotion as the ruling was read out. Peter Ketcheson, Au's counsel, said outside court that the defence respected the judge's decision but "obviously we're disappointed." The legal team plans to digest the ruling before any decisions are made about an appeal, he said.
No date has yet been set for sentencing.

Woollcombe's decision comes more than four years after the fateful April 26, 2021 encounter , when a seemingly mundane exchange turned disastrous. That day, the officer's colleague Const. Gurmakh Benning set out to purchase an Apple watch Facey was selling on Kijiji, and brought along Au for the transaction. After they realized the watch was fake, the off-duty cops chased Facey down, before Au tackled him to the ground.

Immediately afterward, Facey's health rapidly declined: a friend testified at trial that Facey appeared "roughed up" and "exhausted" moments after the clash , and was soon rushed to hospital, confused and complaining he couldn't feel his legs.
Facey died that night from an "intracerebral hemorrhage," or a brain bleed.

Au was originally charged with manslaughter and aggravated assault in Facey's death. But an 11th-hour change in forensic pathology opinion saw prosecutors downgrade those charges to a single count of assault causing bodily harm two weeks before the trial was set to begin. The change meant prosecutors were no longer alleging Au caused Facey's death, something Facey's mother called "heartbreaking."
At the outset her judgment, Woollcombe acknowledged that Facey died just hours after the incident, yet she was not examining the question of how and why that happened.
Nonetheless, Facey's death "loomed over this trial," she said.
"I have no doubt that the loss of Chadd Facey, a young man who had his life ahead of him, still weighs heavily on the hearts and minds of his family and friends," the judge said.

At a week-long trial held in September, prosecutors argued that when Au tackled Facey it was an excessive use of force by the 185-pound cop, who outweighed the "very skinny" Facey by nearly 60 pounds. The unarmed Facey posed "no threat of harm to anyone," Crown prosecutor Sean Horgan argued, and Au had other options available to him other than taking him to the ground.
The tackle instead amounted to street justice , the prosecutor suggested, saying he'd taken Facey down "to teach him a lesson."

Taking the stand in his own defence, Au disagreed, testifying that he used a reasonable amount of force , not a "football tackle," when he took Facey down. Au also told the court that although he was off-duty, he was acting in his capacity as a police officer and was planning to arrest Facey in order to get Benning's money back.
Woollcombe did not believe Au, saying that beyond instructing Facey to stop as he was chasing him, he failed to take basic actions that would indicate he was making an arrest.
"He could have told Facey he was a police officer. He could have said he was arresting him," the judge said.
The judge noted that two experienced officers had been "tricked by a 19-year-old" and they had to be feeling "at least foolish and determined to get back what was rightfully theirs."

At trial, Au had been combative with the Crown prosecutor, often responding to his questions with other questions. Woollcombe was pointedly critical of Au, calling him a "very poor" and "incredible and unreliable witness" who gave "bizarre" answers.
"His evidence as a whole can accurately be characterized as unclear, evasive and argumentative," the judge said.

She also raised concerns about the testimony of Benning, Au's colleague, saying he frequently contradicted his own testimony when he was under cross-examination by Au's defence lawyer, seeming to "go out of his way to assist Au."
She also pushed back on "unhelpful" video re-enactments Au's defence team showed at trial, depicting what they said was Au's takedown, noting the actor playing Facey was taller and heavier than him.

Au is suspended with pay from the Toronto police. He and Benning separately face multiple professional misconduct charges connected to the incident - including for failing to identify themselves as police officers when they called 911 to report the incident, before telling the dispatcher it was resolved. Those charges have been put on hold pending the criminal trial.

Clayton Campbell, president of the Toronto Police Association, called the incident "a tragic case for everyone involved," noting the union's goal was to ensure Au was "treated fairly throughout the process."
"We will continue to do that as we head into sentencing and, eventually, the internal disciplinary process that will follow," he said.
